title: Price tag or auction?
hook: Auctions make buyers compete. Do they always beat a well-chosen price tag?

doesNotKnow: that a seller who knows only the range of values earns more from the best fixed price with one or two bidders, but from an auction once there are three

misconception: An auction always earns more than a fixed price, because buyers compete.
objective: The learner can explain that with values spread evenly from $0 to $100, the best price tag out-earns a second-price auction with 1 or 2 bidders and the auction wins from 3 bidders on, because the auction's price is set by the second-highest bidder and rises with every rival, while a tag is a guess.

claims.text: With n bidders whose values are random and evenly spread from $0 to $100, the best price tag sells when any bidder values the item at the tag or more; it is $50.00, $57.74, $63.00 and $66.87 for 1 to 4 bidders and earns $25.00, $38.49, $47.25 and $53.50 on average.
claims.source: Revenue of a tag p (as a share of $100) is p(1 - p^n), maximised at p = (1/(n + 1))^(1/n). tagPrice() rounds to the cent, tagRevenue() in src/demos/economics/price-tag-or-auction/model.ts; builder's node run: 50, 57.74, 63, 66.87 and 25.00, 38.49, 47.247, 53.499. Brief check J12 (node company/courses/ncm/checks/rejudged-four.mjs) gives the same to one decimal (38.5, 47.2, 53.5). Builder-written; unverified.

claims.text: A second-price auction with no reserve price earns the second-highest value, on average 100(n - 1)/(n + 1) dollars: $0.00, $33.33, $50.00 and $60.00 for 1 to 4 bidders, so it first earns more than the best tag at 3 bidders.
claims.source: Expected second-highest of n uniform values on [0, 100] is 100(n - 1)/(n + 1). auctionRevenue() in model.ts. Comparison with c1: 0 < 25, 33.33 < 38.49, 50.00 > 47.25, 60.00 > 53.50 (and the auction stays ahead: n = 5 gives 66.67 against 58.24 in the builder's node run). J12 auctionFirstWinsAt 3. Builder-written; unverified.

claims.text: The stage's 1,000 simulated sales (seed 7) land near these averages, and 100,000 simulated sales land within $0.20 of each.
claims.source: simulate() in model.ts with the kit's mulberry32(7), not chosen for its result. Builder's run (scratch script loading model.ts with the kit's random.ts): 1,000 sales, tag / auction: n=1 $27.00 / $0.00; n=2 $38.74 / $33.04; n=3 $45.93 / $50.30; n=4 $52.69 / $59.33. 100,000 sales: n=1 $25.03 / $0.00; n=2 $38.50 / $33.27; n=3 $47.20 / $49.95; n=4 $53.49 / $60.00 (largest gap $0.065). Builder-recorded run; unverified.

claims.text: A tag is a guess: too high and nobody buys, too low and money is left on the table. An auction lets the second-highest bidder set the price, and that gets better with every rival.
claims.source: Tag revenue p(1 - p^n): at a high p the chance of no sale (p^n) is large, at a low p the seller gets p even when buyers would pay more (c1). The second-price auction's price is the second-highest value, whose average 100(n - 1)/(n + 1) rises with n (c2). Builder-written; unverified.

claims.text: Auctions are most useful when the seller does not know what buyers will pay.
claims.source: Easley and Kleinberg (2010), Networks, Crowds, and Markets, ch. 9 (section 9.2 unconfirmed: when are auctions appropriate). Carried by the lesson's setup (the seller knows only the $0 to $100 range) and the objective; not a sentence on the card. Attribution: fact-checker confirms.

claims.text: Auctions make buyers compete (hook): in a second-price auction the winner pays what the strongest rival bid.
claims.source: The second-price rule as defined in the prerequisite lesson economics/bid-what-its-worth: the highest bidder wins and pays the second-highest bid. Builder-written; unverified.

recall.question: You sell one concert ticket. You know only that buyers value it somewhere from $0 to $100, and two people are interested. Which tends to earn more?
recall.why: With only two bidders the second-highest value is often low, so the auction earns about $33 on average, while a tag near $58 earns about $38. From three bidders on, the auction wins.
